source.title: Superposition as Lossy Compression: Measure with Sparse Autoencoders and Connect to Adversarial Vulnerability
source.authors: Leonard F. Bereska; Zoe Tzifa-Kratira; Reza Samavi; E. Gavves

page_placements.theme: Superposition and interpretability measures change over training

record.tranche_reason: The study measures superposition with an SAE-activation entropy metric rather than the original toy-model weight measure, and tests how the measured quantity varies with sparsity, task complexity, capacity and training.
record.gate_note: The study measures effective feature counts and compression, not individual neurons’ responses to unrelated inputs or the proportion of polysemantic neurons. Pythia-70M layer-wise feature counts therefore do not test V2. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows. Rows below report the study’s own measurements; the reported SAE and task results are not evidence about specific neuron meanings.
record.test_reason: The study builds and validates a superposition metric (ψ = effective SAE features per neuron) and applies it to dropout, Tracr, grokking, Pythia-70M and adversarial training. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, or what share of neurons is polysemantic. V3 is a causal claim linking superposition to neuron polysemanticity. The study measures only the proposed cause (ψ), not the effect, so no row tests any version. The authors also separate the two constructs, saying polysemanticity can arise without superposition. The toy-model sparsity result (r1) validates their metric against Elhage et al.'s toy models. Its findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it omits the main contribution. The authors present an entropy-on-SAE-activations measure of superposition as lossy compression (ψ = F/N) as their primary contribution, calling the application findings preliminary. They find adversarial training does not universally reduce superposition: abundance regimes (simple task, high capacity) expand features, and scarcity regimes reduce them.
record.recipe_differences: Uses entropy of SAE activation magnitudes to estimate effective feature counts, and applies the measure to toy models, trained networks and adversarial-training settings; it does not use the original neuron-response examples or the Softmax Linear Units intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-count outcomes vary with task complexity, network capacity, layer, dropout rate and adversarial-training strength. The paper also reports sensitivity to SAE regularization and dictionary size, and notes sensitivity to the activation distribution used for measurement; the clean-versus-adversarial gap is described as unpredictable.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, increasing sparsity raises ψ from 1 to 2.5, with growing off-diagonal interference. The SAE-entropy metric tracks this (r = 0.94).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature sparsity drives superposition (features per dimension) in toy bottleneck models.

fits_no_version.finding: Compressed Tracr and scratch-trained transformers on reversal and sorting stay at ψ ≤ 1. Further compression collapses performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dense algorithmic tasks resist superposition beyond the lossless limit.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout monotonically reduces effective features (up to 50%) and accuracy in sparse-parity MLPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout reduces superposition even though it is said to induce polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial training's effect on effective features depends on task complexity (negative slope) and capacity (positive slope).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training does not universally reduce superposition; its direction depends on the task-demand-to-capacity ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-70M, effective SAE feature counts are non-monotonic across layers, with MLPs highest and early MLPs peaking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-wise superposition in language models follows a hunchback pattern like intrinsic dimensionality.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective feature count consolidates sharply at the grokking transition and correlates with LLC (r = 0.908).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition measures track developmental phase transitions.

record.problems: The authors describe the application findings as preliminary and exploratory. The measure depends on SAE quality and choices, has stated feature-splitting, merging and ghost-feature risks, and relies on assumptions about linear, sparse, independent features. The study itself notes that effective feature counts are a proxy rather than literal feature counts. Several aggregate effects are reported without individual condition values, and the clean-versus-adversarial count gap is unpredictable. No direct individual-neuron polysemanticity measurement is provided.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No vision-model neurons or image responses examined.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models. Pythia-70M gives only SAE effective-feature counts per layer.
Superposition (ψ) is measured, but neuron polysemanticity is not, so the causal link is not tested.
Polysemanticity from dropout or regularization is only cited (Marshall & Kirchner; Lecomte et al.), not measured.
Dropout, adversarial training and width are varied, but the share of polysemantic neurons is not measured. SoLU is only proposed as future work.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined.
SAE hyperparameter sensitivity concerns their ψ metric, not neuron polysemanticity classifications.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this as testing V3 (T2), but the study measures superposition, not neuron polysemanticity. The authors explicitly distinguish the two, saying polysemanticity can arise without superposition, so any V3 verdict would rest on an unmeasured link. Pythia figures conflict: 5,600 effective features in the text versus 10,000 / 20× in the Figure 6a caption. Elhage et al.'s Toy Models of Superposition is not among the listed originals.

versions.untested_parts: No individual vision-model neurons or their responses to image inputs are measured.
Pythia-70M is measured for layer-wise SAE feature counts, not the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.

The study measures effective features per neuron and investigates sparsity and capacity, but does not directly identify polysemantic neurons or establish that their mixed responses are caused by superposition.
No test isolates initialization, regularization or training noise as causes of neuron-level polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.

The study varies dropout, adversarial training, architecture and capacity, but measures effective feature counts rather than the share of polysemantic neurons. It does not test SoLU or whether lowering that share preserves performance.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined for a shared feature or related offshoots using improved neuron-level tools.

The study discusses sensitivity of its feature-count proxy to activation distributions and SAE choices, but does not test neuron-level polysemantic classifications across activation ranges or explanation scores.

rows.subject: toy model of superposition (100 models; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied feature sparsity and measured superposition and interference in the toy model.
rows.measure: Superposition and interference as sparsity increases
rows.baseline: low-sparsity models: diagonal dominance with minimal off-diagonal interference
rows.value: As sparsity increases, features pack into shared dimensions; off-diagonal interference grows as ψ increases from 1 to 2.5 (Figure 2b).
rows.note: This is a controlled toy-model result about superposition, not a direct count of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Measures superposition (ψ, W^T W interference) in a metric-validation replication of the toy model. It does not measure neuron polysemanticity, so it cannot show V3's causal link.

rows.subject: compiled Tracr models and transformers trained from scratch (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: compiled or trained from scratch, as applicable
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective feature counts while progressively compressing residual-stream dimensions.
rows.measure: Effective feature count relative to residual-stream width
rows.value: Both compiled models and transformers trained from scratch converge to 12 features; ψ approaches 1 at the F=N boundary, with further compression reducing features and eventually causing performance collapse rather than ψ > 1.
rows.note: The authors attribute resistance to superposition to the lack of sparse activation patterns in sequence operations.
rows.check: Effective feature count vs residual width in Tracr reversal. This is a superposition measure, not polysemantic neurons. 'Partial' has no version-referent.

rows.subject: compiled Tracr models and transformers trained from scratch (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: compiled or trained from scratch, as applicable
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective feature counts while progressively compressing residual-stream dimensions.
rows.measure: Effective feature count relative to residual-stream width
rows.value: Both compiled models and transformers trained from scratch converge to 10 features; F ≈ N throughout compression, with further reduction causing performance degradation and collapse rather than ψ > 1.
rows.note: The study says these algorithmic tasks likely lack the input sparsity needed for lossy compression.
rows.check: Same as r2 for sorting. It measures ψ, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: MLPs on multi-task sparse parity (aggregate across widths)
rows.stage_stated: trained; dropout applied to hidden activations
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective feature counts across dropout rates.

conditions.value: multi-task sparse parity, 3 tasks and 4 bits per task

rows.value: Dropout monotonically reduces effective features, by up to 50%.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as redundant encoding consuming capacity and leaving room for fewer features.
rows.check: Dropout reduces effective SAE features. The authors explicitly say this differs from dropout-induced polysemanticity, which they cite but do not measure.

rows.subject: MLPs on multi-task sparse parity (aggregate across widths)
rows.stage_stated: trained; dropout applied to hidden activations
rows.operation_detail: Measured accuracy across dropout rates alongside feature counts.

conditions.value: multi-task sparse parity, 3 tasks and 4 bits per task

rows.note: This capability result is relevant context for the feature-count reduction; the text gives no numeric accuracy values.
rows.check: Accuracy-only capability row, with no polysemanticity measure and no numeric values.

rows.subject: MLPs and CNNs (meta-analysis aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied adversarial training strength and measured normalized slopes of effective feature counts.

conditions.value: number of classes and dataset difficulty

rows.measure: Relationship between task complexity and normalized feature-count change per unit adversarial-training strength
rows.value: Negative relationship: slope = −0.745 ± 0.122, z = −6.14, p < 0.001; higher task complexity shifts effects from expansion toward reduction.
rows.note: Random-effects modeling was used because of significant heterogeneity.
rows.check: Tests the superposition–adversarial-vulnerability hypothesis, not any polysemantic-neuron version.

rows.subject: adversarially trained networks (aggregate across architectures and datasets)
rows.operation_detail: Compared effective feature counts across adversarial-training strengths for binary-classification tasks.
rows.measure: Effective feature count relative to ϵ = 0 baseline
rows.value: Positive slopes; feature counts expand up to 2× baseline.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across tested conditions; individual condition values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Adversarial-training effect on effective feature count. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: adversarially trained networks (aggregate across architectures and datasets)
rows.operation_detail: Compared effective feature counts across adversarial-training strengths for ten-class tasks.
rows.measure: Effective feature count relative to ϵ = 0 baseline
rows.value: Negative slopes; feature counts decrease by up to 60%, particularly in early layers.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across tested conditions; individual condition values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Adversarial-training effect on effective feature count. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: adversarially trained networks (aggregate across architectures and datasets)
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature counts at several adversarial-training strengths for three-class tasks.
rows.measure: Effective feature count relative to ϵ = 0 baseline
rows.value: Inverted-U pattern: moderate training at ϵ = 0.1 initially expands features, while stronger training at ϵ = 0.3 triggers reduction below baseline.
rows.note: The text does not give individual values for the two strengths.
rows.check: Adversarial-training effect on effective feature count. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: adversarially trained networks on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalized feature-count slopes across dataset difficulty.
rows.note: Fashion-MNIST produced systematically more negative slopes.
rows.check: Dataset-difficulty effect on adversarial-training slopes. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: single-layer MLPs and CNNs on MNIST (meta-analysis aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied adversarial-training strength and network capacity; measured feature-count slopes.
rows.measure: Relationship between capacity and normalized feature-count slope
rows.value: Positive capacity relationship: meta-analytic slope = 0.220 ± 0.037, z = 5.90, p < 0.001. Narrow networks (8 units/filters) show negative slopes; high-capacity networks (512 units/64 filters) show positive slopes, including for 10-class tasks.
rows.note: The study reports the aggregate relationship and the stated narrow-versus-wide results.
rows.check: Capacity effect on adversarial-training slopes. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Varied adversarial-training strength and width; measured normalized feature-count slopes.
rows.measure: Relationship between width and normalized feature-count slope
rows.value: Log-linear slope = 31.0 ± 2.0 per log(width); an 8-fold width increase produces a 65-unit change in normalized slope. At 0.25× width, training barely affects feature counts; at 2× width, slopes approach 80.
rows.note: The paper reports a strong width-dependent shift toward feature expansion.
rows.check: ResNet width effect on adversarial-training slopes. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective feature-count changes by layer under adversarial training.

conditions.value: conv1, layer1, middle layers, layer3 and layer4

rows.value: Early layers reduce features by up to 50%, middle layers remain stable, and deep layers expand up to 4×; at 1/4 width, late-layer expansion vanishes while early-layer reduction persists but weakens.
rows.note: The direction differs across layers and changes with width.
rows.check: Layer-wise adversarial-training feature changes. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Measured layer- and component-wise effective feature counts from pretrained SAEs.

conditions.value: embedding and attn_out, mlp_out, resid_out for layers 0–5
20,000 text samples; convergence saturation after 2 × 10^4 samples

rows.measure: Effective feature count and layer-wise organization
rows.value: For MLP 1, 21,000 SAE features activate and the entropy measure yields 5,600 effective features; MLPs have the most features, attention the fewest, and counts peak in early layers before declining and re-expanding.
rows.note: This is a layer-wise effective-feature result, not a measurement of mixed neuron responses.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The paper is internally inconsistent: the text gives 5,600 effective features for MLP 1, but the Figure 6a caption says it peaks at 10,000 features (20× neurons).

rows.subject: two-path MLP on modular arithmetic
rows.stage_stated: trained for 25,000 steps; checkpoints every 250 steps
rows.operation_detail: Tracked effective feature count during training and compared it with the Local Learning Coefficient.
rows.measure: Feature-count dynamics and correlation with LLC
rows.baseline: LLC shows initial proliferation followed by smooth decay
rows.value: Feature count shows sharp consolidation at the generalization transition; correlation with LLC is r = 0.908, p < 0.001.
rows.note: A developmental measurement of effective features; not a neuron-level polysemanticity result.

relation.reason: The metric takes the superposition hypothesis (features packed into fewer neurons) and SAE decomposition as its premise. It reports its own measurements without testing whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

tranche.reason: Not a test: it measures superposition (psi = effective SAE features per neuron), a related construct, never neuron-level polysemanticity. It builds its metric on the superposition hypothesis and on SAEs, which it introduces as tools for polysemantic representations. So T4 fits better than T6.

source_check.notes: The paper measures superposition, not polysemantic neurons. In Sec 6.1, dropout lowers effective features while cited work says dropout raises polysemanticity. The authors read this as polysemanticity differing from superposition, which is context for V3/V4 but has no neuron-level measurement. The authors call their application findings preliminary and their counts comparative, not absolute.

statements.correction: Text: feature count shows sharp consolidation at the generalization transition (epoch 60); correlation with LLC r = 0.908, p < 0.001 (Sec 6.3, Fig 6b); two-path MLP on (a + b) mod 53.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Increasing sparsity is accompanied by features sharing dimensions and increased interference as ψ rises from 1 to 2.5 (r1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: algorithmic sequence reversal and sorting tasks
reader_labels.reason: These tasks approach F=N but do not show ψ>1; further compression reduces features and performance, consistent with the authors’ account that sparse activation is needed for superposition (r2, r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: adversarial training across task complexities and capacities
reader_labels.reason: Measured feature-count effects are not universal: task complexity and capacity shift the direction, with expansion in some settings and reduction in others (r6–r13).
